topic.title: Thomas Lipton, a Glasgow Grocer, Bought Tea Gardens in Ceylon

title: Your Lipton Tea Bag Is Named After a Glasgow Shopkeeper
description:
Whose name is on your tea bag? A Glasgow shopkeeper's.
Thomas Lipton opened a grocery in Glasgow, went to Ceylon and bought tea gardens, and his name outlived the shop.
Sources: Grace's Guide, NPR, The Grocer (Nov 2021).
Based on public records and reporting. Not financial or legal advice.

lines.text: Your Lipton tea bag is named after a shopkeeper from Glasgow.
That shopkeeper, Thomas Lipton, ended up owning tea gardens on the other side of the world. So how does a grocer get tea gardens?
He opened his first Glasgow shop in 1871, and he wanted no middlemen between him and his customers.
So in 1890 he went to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, and bought tea estates of his own.
His packs promised tea straight from his gardens, and his name went up over the factory.
But his gardens could never fill every pack. NPR found he bought from brokers too, and only a small part came from his own estates.
The name stuck anyway. In the end, Unilever sold the tea business that held Lipton, 34 brands in all, for €4.5B.
His own gardens or the brokers: which one filled your cup? Either way, look closely, because

Beat 'hook', params.layers[0].lines: the card is typeset as a Grace's Guide RECORD, so every line reads as that source's text, but the page can't be opened (503) and two claims are not confirmed. (a) 'selling ham, butter and eggs cheaply': sources tie ham, butter and eggs to his parents' Crown Street shop (Wikipedia, Undiscovered Scotland). For his own Stobcross Street shop only blogs and picture captions say hams and dairy, and no two reputable outlets agree. (b) 'was born in Glasgow to Irish parents': his birthplace and date are disputed (historian James MacKay doubts Lipton's own account; the topic's verify list keeps the birth details out), and the parents are recorded as Ulster-Scots from County Fermanagh. Fix: cut the card to lines the sources confirm, e.g. 'Thomas Lipton, grocer, opened his first shop, Lipton's Market, in Stobcross Street, Glasgow, in {fact1}' plus, if wanted, 'After some years in America...', 'His shops spread across Britain' and the Ceylon line, all confirmed. Or drop the Grace's Guide record styling. Everything else re-checked and confirmed: the 'No middlemen' label (start) matches the narration and NPR (he wanted to stop buying from brokers); the Lipton Ice Tea glass (gardens) and the NYPL 'Tea Estate with Pluckers' postcard (brokers) show no claim and fit their lines; all 4 sourced facts as in the earlier pass.
